title: Should a UGC hook mention the product at all?
description: When a UGC hook should mention the product, when holding it back works better, how to decide per video, and how to ask the brand which opening it wants.
short_answer: A UGC hook can mention the product when the product itself is the surprise, but leave it out when the viewer needs to recognise a problem first. Decide by what your first line promises, and ask the brand whether it wants the product named in the opening, because a brief can settle the choice for you.

sections.heading: When does naming the product in the hook help?

blocks.text: Name the product in the hook when the product is the thing worth stopping for: an odd shape, a new idea, or something the viewer has never seen.

In those cases the product is the question the viewer wants answered, so hiding it wastes your strongest line. A [hook](/glossary/#hook) like I didn't know you could get a kettle that folds flat works because the product and the surprise are the same thing. Every hook pattern in [the guide to writing a UGC hook](/how-to-write-a-hook/) still applies; you are just choosing the product as the subject.

items: Say what the product is in plain words, such as a folding kettle, rather than its full name, unless the brief asks for the name.
Pair the mention with the reason it is interesting, because a product type on its own gives the viewer nothing to wonder about.
Keep the line short enough to say in one breath, so the product does not crowd out the hook itself.

sections.heading: When does mentioning the product too early hurt?

blocks.text: Mentioning it early hurts when the viewer has to care about the problem before the product means anything to them.

A product the viewer has never heard of is just a word in the first second, and a first line that sounds like a pitch gives a viewer who feels sold to a reason to leave. Opening on a situation they recognise earns the product a place later. It also gives you a cleaner [payoff](/glossary/#payoff), because the video sets up a problem and then answers it, which is the balance covered in [hook and payoff](/blog/hook-payoff/).

Saying the product and showing it are separate choices. You can keep it in frame from the start and still not name it until later; [hooking a video when the product is in the first frame](/blog/product-first-frame-hook/) covers the visual side, so this answer sticks to what you say.

sections.heading: How do you decide for a specific video?

blocks.text: Decide by asking what the viewer needs first, the product or the problem, and then check that against the brief.

table_head: Mention the product in the hook?
table_rows: The product looks unusual or does something unexpected
The product is the surprise, so it carries the hook.
It solves a problem the viewer may not notice yet
The viewer needs a reason to care before the product lands.
The brief gives a required opening line
The brand has made the call, so your job is to make that line sound natural.
The brand says the ad is for people already comparing options
Those viewers are looking for the category, so naming it tells them they are in the right place.
The brand can choose from two real openings instead of a description of one.

blocks.text: If the video is an ad, ask the brand who it is for before you choose, and read [what makes a UGC hook work in an ad](/blog/ugc-ad-hooks/) for the questions that shape an ad opening.

sections.heading: What does a hook that holds the product back sound like?

blocks.text: It names the situation in the first line and brings the product in at the turn, once the viewer wants an answer.

In the script below the product is never named until [the turn](/glossary/#the-turn), and even then it is called what it is, not given a brand name. Swap the hook for a product-first line and the rest still works, which is useful if the brand wants both.

blocks.script_caption: Example script — written for this answer, for a silicone baking mat

script_beats.say: Every batch of cookies I bake leaves a layer of itself welded to the tray.
script_beats.do: Close shot of a baking tray with cookie bits stuck on, a spatula scraping at them.

script_beats.say: I've been lining it with paper, and I still end up soaking the tray overnight.
script_beats.do: Creator holds up a crumpled sheet of baking paper next to the tray sitting in the sink.

script_beats.say: So tonight I'm trying something different.
script_beats.do: Creator takes a rolled-up mat out of a drawer and unrolls it onto a clean tray.

script_beats.say: This is a silicone baking mat. It lies flat on the tray, so there's no cutting and no paper.
script_beats.do: Hand presses the mat flat; the camera tilts to show it covering the tray edge to edge.

script_beats.say: Same dough, same oven, same timer as last time.
script_beats.do: Creator spoons dough onto the mat and slides the tray into the oven.

script_beats.say: And tonight they lifted straight off. No scraping.
script_beats.do: Close shot as baked cookies are lifted off the mat with a spatula, the mat visible underneath.

script_beats.say: It rolls back up into the drawer. The one I used is linked.
script_beats.do: Creator rinses the mat, rolls it up and puts it back in the drawer.

sections.heading: Should you ask the brand which opening it prefers?

blocks.text: Ask before you film, because a brief can require the product name in the first line or rule it out, and guessing wrong means a reshoot.

Check the [brief](/glossary/#brief) first; if it says nothing about the opening, a one-line question settles it: For the opening, would you like [PRODUCT] named in the first line, or should I open on the problem and bring it in later? I can film both if that helps.

Offering both can be the simplest answer. Film the product-first hook and the problem-first hook against the same body, label them clearly, and let the brand choose. [How many hooks to film for one video](/blog/ugc-hook-variations/) explains how to plan those versions so they join the rest of the video cleanly.

hooks: Every batch of cookies I bake leaves a layer of itself welded to the tray.
